5.text: Another case happened almost in my own presence. I was on my way

6.text: from the Russian villages on the Lower Kolyma into the heart of the tundra,

7.text: together with some Chukchee fellow-travellers. They had made a visit to

8.text: the Russian settlements for trading-purposes, and were now returning to their

9.text: camps. Among them was one Ñĭroˊn, a young man of violent and disorderly

10.text: temper. His name has been mentioned before.¹ Instead of trading, he lost

11.text: everything in card-playing, among other things some fawn-skins sent with him

12.text: for sale by his neighbors in camp. Even one of his reindeer went the same

13.text: way, and now he drove a single reindeer. He was a good walker, however,

14.text: and during most of the time ran in front of our train as fleet and active as

15.text: any reindeer-buck. One evening, when we were approaching his camp, we

16.text: were told that the sister of Ñĭroˊn, who usually staid at home, had left the

17.text: house and gone to one Meˊwet, a man with whom Ñĭroˊn had had a quarrel.

18.text: The young woman had already been twice divorced, and the quarrel between

19.text: her brother and Meˊwet, as far as I know, was on her account. Receiving

20.text: this information, Ñĭroˊn became so angered that he took his spear and a long

21.text: girdle-knife and started that very night for the camp of Meˊwet. His sledge,

22.text: and reindeer he left behind, and went on afoot, eager for vengeance. Nothing

23.text: very terrible, however, happened. Ñĭroˊn was quite poor, and Meˊwet had a

24.text: good-sized herd; and the next year, when I met Ñĭroˊn again in a Russian

25.text: village on the Kolyma, he was gambling as usual, and part of the stake

26.text: were the fawn-skins sent for sale by Meˊwet, his new brother-in-law.

27.text: Mixed Marriages. — The Reindeer Chukchee, at least at the present

28.text: time, are fond of marrying women of other tribes. “We want to know their

29.text: taste,” the aforementioned ᴇˊttɪhɪn told me rather cynically; “we are connois-

30.text: seurs.” On the Koryak frontier, both Reindeer tribes — the Chukchee and the

31.text: Koryak — easily mix together in marriage; the more so, as life and language

32.text: are very much alike. Therefore some groups of families are of quite mixed

33.text: blood, and cannot even tell to what tribe they really belong. The distinction

34.text: is the more difficult, as the Reindeer Chukchee and the Reindeer Koryak

35.text: call themselves in a similar way Čauˊču, and call each other Taˊn˙ñɪtan.² Mixed

36.text: marriages between the Chukchee and Reindeer Chuvantzy also take place

37.text: freely. Mixed marriages between the Reindeer Chukchee and the Maritime

38.text: Chukchee and Eskimo, as stated before, happen quite frequently. I know a

39.text: couple of dozen cases of marriage between the Chukchee and the Tungus or

40.text: Lamut. This comes about in two ways. According to the first method, a

41.text: rich Chukchee marries a young Tungus girl, paying her price in live reindeer,
